title: Landmark Crimea bridge hit as Russia reports biggest Ukrainian drone attack of war
description: Russia says it has recorded the biggest Ukrainian drone attack since the war began, in which a landmark bridge linking Russia to occupied Crimea susta
body: Russia says it has recorded the biggest Ukrainian drone attack since the war began, in which a landmark bridge linking Russia to occupied Crimea sustained minor damage and several oil refineries were hit.The Russian military intercepted and destroyed 2,049 drones and four Flamingo long-distance missiles over 24 hours, officials said. Around 600 flew towards the capital alone, Moscow Mayor Sergey Sobyanin added.Kyiv, meanwhile, came under a record 17 air raid alerts in a single day. At least seven people were killed by Russian strikes and attacks on energy infrastructure caused blackouts for 50,000 people. The intense strikes come days after US, Ukrainian and Russian envoys held talks aimed at ending the war. The war in Ukraine began with Russia's full-scale invasion in February 2022.The Moscow-installed head of Crimea, Sergei Aksyonov, confirmed that drones had struck the Crimean Bridge connecting Russia with the annexed peninsula, leading to traffic restrictions.The structure - also known as Kerch Bridge - was built by Russia after it invaded and annexed the peninsula in 2014. It was inaugurated by Russian President Vladimir Putin to great fanfare in 2018 and is carefully protected with multiple layers of aerial and maritime defences. Russian pro-war military commentators said on Telegram that rather than a direct attack, the bridge had suffered from the impact of drone warhead debris. Neither Ukraine's domestic security service nor its main military intelligence directorate  has responded to a BBC request for comment. Atesh, a partisan Ukrainian group operating inside Russian-held territory, said on social media that authorities in Crimea were "bracing for further strikes" on the Kerch Bridge and that they felt Moscow did not appreciate the seriousness of the situation.Ukrainian drones also hit several energy facilities, including an oil refinery in Ilsky, in the southern Krasnodar region, where falling drone debris sparked a fire and injured six people, including children.Last week, President Volodymyr Zelensky accused Russia of carrying out a concerted operation against Ukraine's bridges in order to "divide Ukraine... and make life as difficult as possible for people" on both sides of the Dnipro River which cuts across the country.Despite the high-level diplomacy and visits by US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff to both Putin and Zelensky, peace remains a distant prospect. Moscow is uncompromising on its demands for Ukraine to cede territory and give up efforts to become a Nato member. The Kremlin has now also started to talk again about the need to rethink Europe's "security architecture", often intended by Moscow to mean a scaled-down Nato presence in countries close to Russia. The apparent willingness of the US to engage in this conversation has set off alarm bells among Ukraine's European partners, which are concerned their continent's security could be redrawn by Washington and Moscow without their involvement.A team of six - Britain, France, Germany, Italy, Poland and a representative of the EU institutions - will represent Europe in future talks with Russia, Ukraine and the US. But the Kremlin continues to be dismissive of European input. "We have also said more than once we need to understand... how much their position will help the peace process," said spokesman Dmitri Peskov. EU representatives kept pushing for "unconditional support" for Ukraine and "enhanced pressure" on Russia, Peskov said, adding that "this sort of wording rather suggests their reluctance to facilitate the peace process".

schema.headline: Landmark Crimea bridge hit as Russia reports biggest Ukrainian drone attack of war

title: Emma Barnett: Host to leave Radio 4's Today and start new BBC show
description: Radio 4 presenter Emma Barnett is set to leave the Today programme this week for a multiplatform new BBC show in the New Year.Former Woman's Hour host
body: Radio 4 presenter Emma Barnett is set to leave the Today programme this week for a multiplatform new BBC show in the New Year.Former Woman's Hour host Barnett has developed a "bold" new show, she says, which will launch in 2027 across BBC Sounds, BBC iPlayer and YouTube.Her final day presenting Radio 4's flagship morning news and current affairs show will be on Wednesday 18 November."For the last nearly six years - it's been incredible to talk to the mighty Radio 4 listeners," she said in a statement. "Having proudly hosted Woman's Hour and now the Today Programme - I've had the rare pleasure of hosting nearly every hour of the morning on this truly unique and special radio network."She added: "But it's not goodbye to the BBC audience I value so greatly because I have something else for them that I hope will add something meaningful and entertaining to their lives."Posting on Instagram, external, she said there would be more information on what her new show would be about soon."Watch this space and look ready. I am… More soon."Barnett joined Today in May 2024, taking over from Martha Kearney to work alongside co-presenters Nick Robinson, Mishal Husain, Amol Rajan and Justin Webb. Husain and Rajan have since left.Today programme editor Rebecca Keating said Barnett had brought "enormous energy" to Today, with "a keen focus" on listeners.She noted how Barnett had a proven "track record of telling stories of personal hardship that influence public debate" but how she was "also equally at home interviewing British icons like Dame Judi Dench."We will miss her generous tea making and wish her every success in her new venture."In August, Barnett, 41, revealed she had had a hysterectomy and surgery for endometriosis, days before a documentary she made about the condition was broadcast.She returned to the Today programme explaining she had been absent in recent weeks because she was in hospital "in a case of life imitating work".Speaking on her BBC podcast, Ready to Talk with Emma Barnett, last year, she told listeners that finding out she was going through perimenopause at the age of 38 felt like she had been "mugged, robbed".The broadcaster said it was the "first time in my life I haven't really wanted to be a woman - it's the first time I've thought, I'd really quite like to be a bloke".Radio 4 controller Mohit Bakaya said he was "delighted she's staying with the BBC" and would "look forward to her new show."

schema.headline: Emma Barnett: Host to leave Radio 4's Today and start new BBC show

title: Aged 16-24 and looking for work? Use our look-up to find out which areas have the most jobs
description: Image source, Getty ImagesByTommy LumbyBusiness data journalist and Nick EdserBusiness reporterIf you're one of the nearly one million people aged 16-
body: Image source, Getty ImagesByTommy LumbyBusiness data journalist and Nick EdserBusiness reporterIf you're one of the nearly one million people aged 16-24 not in education, employment or training - otherwise known as "Neet" - then you might be wondering where to start.Under-25s should be guaranteed job placements or training to help them find permanent work, a major review aimed at cutting the number of Neets will say.But how many jobs are there where you live and in which sectors are you most likely to find an opening?How many job vacancies are there?There is no official measure of how many vacancies are suitable for young people, but across the whole economy there were 691,000 jobs available in the July to September period this year, which is the lowest number since early 2021.The Covid pandemic led to huge swings in the number of job vacancies available as companies reacted to shutdowns and then reopened as restrictions were lifted.Stripping out the fluctuations seen during the pandemic, the number of vacancies is now at its lowest level for 12 years.Apprenticeships have often been a way for people to get their first taste of employment.In England the number of people starting apprenticeships has risen in recent years, although this has been driven by an increase in those aged 25 and over after schemes for older workers were fully rolled out in 2008.The number of people aged 24 and under starting apprenticeships in England in 2025 was 172,230, down from a recent peak of 291,300 in 2012.Where are the available jobs?Where you live will often have a big impact on your ability to find a job.We have used online job adverts to help identify the number of vacancies suitable for young people in the area they live, relative to the size of the local population.The Institute for Public Policy Research (IPPR) think tank used AI to help identify the jobs, which were broadly defined as roles requiring relatively low experience or education.According to its analysis, South Oxfordshire had 387 suitable vacancies per 1,000 18 to 24-year-olds in the area - the most of any local authority. Rotherham had the least, at 53 per 1,000.Use this tool to check out the situation in your area. The data for London is only available for the region as a whole and is not broken down by individual councils.Which sectors have the most entry-level jobs?Even if there are jobs available in your area, you might not find one in the sector you want to work in.The sector with the highest average number of entry-level vacancies in the year to October was teaching, with most of those jobs being for teaching assistants, learning support and cover supervisor roles, according to jobs website Adzuna.The next largest was hospitality and catering, traditionally an area where younger people get their first experience of work.Adzuna, a major online jobs website, includes adverts for full-time roles marked as entry-level, those asking for up to two years' experience, graduate roles, internships and apprenticeships.Accounting and finance had the third-highest number of job openings.What are the typical rates of pay?Figures on salaries for vacancies can be patchy because many employers do not include them in job adverts.Prime Minister Andy Burnham recently urged businesses to start publishing salaries ahead of plans to make pay details compulsory in adverts.Only about 40% of Adzuna's jobs data for the year to October stated a salary, although that figure varies widely by sector.Here are the average salaries for jobs in the sectors with the largest number of entry-level jobs, according to Adzuna. The highest average salary is £30,530 in engineering, while social care has the lowest at £25,880.

schema.headline: Aged 16-24 and looking for work? Use our look-up to find out which areas have the most jobs

title: Children dropping out of school: What can politicians do about it?
description: The stories of Eva and Mali - which you can watch in the video above - and the many teenagers like them who don't go to school, either regularly or at
body: The stories of Eva and Mali - which you can watch in the video above - and the many teenagers like them who don't go to school, either regularly or at all, strike to the heart of one of the many big challenges the Milburn Review is seeking to address.The government-commissioned work, led by former Labour cabinet minister Alan Milburn, is looking into how to solve the problem of nearly one million young people not being in employment, education or training, or Neet.A key challenge is addressing the issue of school absence. The government believes around a third of young people who are persistently absent in Years 10 and 11 in England go on to be Neet, compared with 10% of those who are not persistently absent.Persistent absence almost doubles between Years 7 and 9, reaching around one in four children by Year 9.Thirteen-year-old Eva hadn't been to school for 15 months before September.She described how she used to get up every morning, try to get ready for school and get stuck by the front door.Mali, 18, stopped attending school three years ago when she was in year 10.We shared their stories with the decision makers and those who want to be our decision makers – in other words, those in government and those who would like to be.It offers an insight into the political arguments to come.Labour reckons the Conservatives' education reforms of the last decade and a half served academic high achievers very well but created what one source described as an an "endless treadmill of failure" for some - and so let them down. A government spokesperson said: "When children feel they belong at school, they show up, and when they show up, they achieve."Therefore, the spokesperson added, "the education secretary is driving ambitious reforms to boost attendance" and "intervene earlier when children need support". The Liberal Democrats also sought to pin the blame on the Tories.Munira Wilson, who speaks for the party on education, said "the Conservatives failed to give them the support they needed after lockdown, and years of underinvestment in their recovery are now showing up in rising mental health figures". She added that "every young person should feel they belong".These reactions prompt some of the big questions that arise from Eva and Mali's experiences. Where should responsibility for their situations lie? The individual, the parents, the rules in the pandemic, schools, colleges, mental health provision? Perhaps a combination of all of these things in some instances and other things besides.The Conservatives have pushed back strongly against the criticism from Labour and the Liberal Democrats.Shadow education secretary Laura Trott told the BBC: "We mustn't give up on any child, every day a child misses school sets them back. "Schools are doing great work to bring absence down. Those children who have special education needs or are struggling to leave home, need specialist support and in some cases specialist schools." And she added: "High academic standards lift everyone up. It is insulting to suggest that not all children are capable of good academic outcomes. Too much maths and English are not making young people Neet."Former Conservative cabinet minister Suella Braverman, now Reform UK's education spokesperson, told us: "As someone who co-founded and chaired an outstanding state school with a high proportion of children on free school meals but a below average school absence rate, it is clear that the culture and teaching in a school can make a huge difference."She added that "greater parental engagement" and a "culture of perseverance" were essential too.The government is expected to accept the broad thrust of Alan Milburn's report, before responding in detail in the next month or so. We are told there will be an announcement from Education Secretary Lucy Powell directly relevant to Eva, Mali and the many like them, later this week.

schema.headline: Children dropping out of school: What can politicians do about it?

title: UK has lost more than it gained from Brexit, Andy Burnham says
description: The prime minister has argued the UK has lost more than it has gained from leaving the European Union in a speech ahead of a UK-EU summit later this w
body: The prime minister has argued the UK has lost more than it has gained from leaving the European Union in a speech ahead of a UK-EU summit later this week.Speaking at the Lord Mayor's Banquet on Monday, Andy Burnham compared the UK's Brexit deal to the "emperor's new clothes" - saying "a needlessly hard Brexit" created barriers for businesses and the promise to "take back control" was not delivered.He is due to sign new agreements on food, energy and youth mobility with the bloc at Friday's summit, after the substance of those deals was set by his predecessor Sir Keir Starmer.The Conservatives have said Labour are "dragging us into the European Union via the back door".In his first major speech on foreign policy, the prime minister said that following the summit he would begin new discussions with the EU about options for "our long-term relationship". However, he warned it would take time and insisted that "at every stage the British people will be the boss".Burnham has ruled out major changes before the next general election.On the UK's current relationship with EU, Burnham said: "It's like the emperor's new clothes – where no-one is prepared to say the obvious truth. Well, I say it as I see it. And to be frank, the emperor has nothing on."The Brexit we were given has not worked. We have lost more than we have gained."Ahead of Friday's UK-EU summit, Burnham set out three tests for any agreement.Firstly, that it must be consistent with Labour's 2024 general election manifesto pledge that there would be "no return to the single market, the customs union, or freedom of movement".He also said it must improve the original Brexit deal and bring it closer to what people thought they were voting for in 2016.Finally, he said any deal must pass the "Makerfield test" of providing tangible improvements to people's everyday lives - a reference to voters in Burnham's Greater Manchester constituency.He also said the prospect of a new deal is a "win-win" and illustrates a "new approach"."Not adversarial. No longer burning bridges. But being constructive and positive - showing that we can come together to confront shared challenges."Burnham said "Britain was back in the game in a big way" and would be a country that "leads with its values". As a candidate in the Makerfield by-election that propelled his return to Parliament, Burnham had promised not to "re-run" Brexit arguments and said he was "not proposing that the UK considers rejoining the EU".However, since becoming prime minister he has said he wants to explore a different long-term relationship with the bloc.He has suggested potential options for the future could range from no changes to the UK-EU relationship, to rejoining the customs union, the single market or a fresh referendum on full EU membership.The prime minister has stressed any changes would require a mandate from the public at a general election.Boris Johnson, who was prime minister when the UK left the EU in 2020 and negotiated the original Brexit deal, has warned Burnham against "wasting his premiership" on Europe.He told the Daily Telegraph, external he believed the public would back Brexit again if Burnham forced another vote on the issue."It is madness to escalate the Brexit issue as your political priority," Johnson told the paper."He will impale himself and his party on this point, and he needs to move off it because he won't win – because the reality is that people are not fools."Deputy Conservative leader Alex Burghart accused Burnham of "reopening a debate the country settled long ago, while ignoring the challenges facing Britain today".Reform UK has said one of the "key benefits" of Brexit is that Britain no longer has to "adhere to ridiculous EU rules", and argued that any form of alignment could have a negative impact on the country's trade policy.The Liberal Democrats have said the draft deal on food exports is a "patch, not a fix" and that the "real solution is to re-join the single market and to establish a customs union with the EU".The Green Party of England and Wales has called for the UK to re-join the customs union, with leader Zack Polanski previously saying "full membership of the EU remains the best option for the UK".

schema.headline: UK has lost more than it gained from Brexit, Andy Burnham says

title: Grand Slam of Darts: Luke Littler lands triple-bull checkout, as Gerwyn Price benefits from maths error
description: Gerwyn Price and Luke Littler both made it through to the Grand Slam of Darts knockout stage on a night featuring a bizarre maths error and a sensatio
body: Gerwyn Price and Luke Littler both made it through to the Grand Slam of Darts knockout stage on a night featuring a bizarre maths error and a sensational triple-bull checkout.Littler suffered a 5-4 defeat by Dutchman Niels Zonneveld but claimed the three legs he required to progress from the group stage.The 19-year-old, egged on by the crowd at the Aldersley venue in Wolverhampton, improbably landed three darts on the bullseye to produce a remarkable 150 checkout and level the match at 4-4, only to lose the deciding leg.Price, meanwhile, claimed a 5-2 victory over Sebastian Bialecki - although he was the beneficiary of an unusual mathematical mistake.The Welshman was 2-1 up against Poland's Bialecki and required 135 to win the fourth leg.Price's first dart hit treble 19, leaving him with 78, but he asked referee Charlie Corstorphine what he had left to score and was incorrectly told 88.In good faith, Price promptly threw treble 16 and then double 20 to win the leg, having scored 145 - which should have bust him."A rare scoring error was made by the referee in the fourth leg of the match between Gerwyn Price and Sebastian Bialecki," organisers the PDC told BBC Sport in a statement."Under Darts Regulation Authority (DRA) rule 6.4, as the error was not corrected before the next leg began, the leg score stands as announced."Price said he was unaware of the miscalculation until it was flagged up to him before he walked into a post-match news conference."I hit the first treble and I asked 'what have I got left?' and he said 88, so I threw treble 16 and double top, then he said 'game shot'," said fourth seed Price. "I'm glad I didn't know, because it probably would have played on my mind."

schema.headline: Grand Slam of Darts: Luke Littler lands triple-bull checkout, as Gerwyn Price benefits from maths error

title: Nations Championship: England's Will Joseph in line to start against New Zealand
description: "He is just so fast. He doesn't look too fast in the first two steps and then he is just gone. He gets away from people," said former England wing Chr
body: "He is just so fast. He doesn't look too fast in the first two steps and then he is just gone. He gets away from people," said former England wing Chris Ashton on BBC Radio 5 Live of Joseph's ability."He floats, doesn't he?" added England team-mate Ben Earl to BBC Sport."The way he carries himself, he does really move like his brother. They are so, so similar."With Feyi-Waboso ruled out of the autumn by an ankle injury, Cadan Murley is the other specialist wing in England's squad vying with Joseph for a spot alongside likely first-choice Tommy Freeman in the back three.After victories over Australia and Japan this autumn, England are second in the Nations Championship northern hemisphere standings and in line for a play-off meeting with South Africa on finals weekend on 27-29 November.However, that could change considerably, with New Zealand leading the southern hemisphere table and second-place South Africa taking on Ireland, who are behind England only on points difference.

title: Robert Pattinson: How the Twilight star became 007
description: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Robert Pattinson has starred in films including the Twilight franchise and The Batman ByHelen BushbyCulture r
body: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Robert Pattinson has starred in films including the Twilight franchise and The Batman ByHelen BushbyCulture reporterRobert Pattinson's career is already flying high with roles in films including the Twilight series, The Batman and The Odyssey, so signing up to play James Bond will propel his profile into the stratosphere. He's already established himself as a leading man, action star and character actor, which is clearly why he is about to play the suave, British secret agent 007.At 40, he is slightly older than some of the other men reportedly lined up for the role, but he's also the most famous - something the new Bond studio Amazon-MGM may have favoured, with an eye on the box office. His recent work has garnered both critical and box office success, including Christopher Nolan's summer blockbuster The Odyssey, in which he played the villainous Antinous.Pattinson was also called "Oscar-worthy" by the Independent and "superb" by The Times, for his performance in November's Primetime, as the real-life host of US TV show To Catch a Predator.He also helped lead 2022's The Batman to the second-biggest North American opening of the Covid-19 pandemic behind Spider-Man: No Way Home. The Guardian said he played the "brooding" role with "appealing vulnerability, external". Meanwhile in dark romantic comedy The Drama, he and his co-star gave a "career-highlight performance", external. It's one of three films he appeared in with Zendaya this year, along with The Odyssey and Dune: Part Three.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Robert Pattinson starred in 2022's The Batman, which was described by critics as a grim, gritty, and gripping super-noirBorn in Barnes, south-west London, Pattinson grew up with his father, a classic car trader and mother, who worked at a modelling agency, and two elder sisters. His interest in acting started while he was still at school, when he joined the Barnes Theatre Club."I wouldn't be acting if it wasn't for that little club," he told Your Local Guardian in 2008, external."I went originally because a lot of pretty girls went there," he said. "I worked backstage and I started acting when all the good people left and I was the only one tall enough to play the lead."In a weird sort of way, that stuff was probably the best I've done and the stuff I am most proud of."He landed his first big film role more than two decades ago, playing Cedric Diggory in 2005's Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire. A relatively minor character, but it was enough to get him noticed.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Robert Pattinson and Kristen Stewart starred in five Twilight films from 2005 to 2012Three years later, he had a starring role in the first of five Twilight films, along with Kristen Stewart, in which they played star-crossed lovers - vampire Edward Cullen and mortal-turned vampire Kristen Stewart. Based on Stephanie Meyer's hugely popular young adult books, the films globally grossed more than $3bn (£2.2bn) by 2012, and established Pattinson as a heartthrob. He spoke in his early career of finding his often adoring, screaming fans hard to deal with. "Although is part of the job, it feels like they have been paid to turn up and scream at me at 7.30pm," he said. "Nothing I don't think can prepare you for the fans. I don't know why I'm not getting used to it but I'm completely overwhelmed every time."Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Pattinson and Zendaya have appeared in three films together this year - The Drama, The Odyssey and Dune: Part ThreeThe following year though, he was back in big-studio territory, with Odyssey director Christopher Nolan, in sci-fi thriller Tenet, and again in 2022 with The Batman, directed by Matt Reeves and co-starring Zoe Kravitz and Paul Dano.Pattinson told Screen Daily why he returned to big-budget films, explaining: "I guess I was trying to do the opposite of what I've been doing. I started thinking, 'I really want to do a big thing.' "I hadn't done something with a massive budget for ages. But you approach it exactly the same way."The Batman got generally positive reviews, re-establishing Pattinson with a broader range of fans. By 2025, when he was on the red carpet for Parasite director Bong Joon Ho's sci-fi black comedy, Mickey 17, he said it was "quite strange" to have a fanbase that was now dominated by men, external."There's like a bunch of guys, which is a new one for me!" he told the Associated Press.Pattinson's private life has often created interest in the press, not least his previous relationships with Stewart, and then the singer FKA Twigs. Since 2018, he has been in a relationship with model Suki Waterhouse. They got engaged in December 2023 and had their first child, a daughter, in March.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Robert Pattinson and Suki Waterhouse have been a couple since 2018With his latest role as James Bond, Pattinson will be extremely busy, not least because the forthcoming Batman sequel is reportedly due out in 2028. But the actor will have a head start as 007, having already worked with Bond 26 director Denis Villeneuve, who also helmed Dune: Part Three. Pattinson was full of praise for him on their most recent film, despite the strain of working in the furnace-like heat of the desert. "The scale of this stuff is just unbelievable, you're having your own Dune theme park, where the gimbal is going upside down and flying, and this is not like work at all," he told the New York Times, external."There are no negatives. Apart from having your sweat drained out of the top of your head, and getting like bulbous sweat bubbles. But even then, I didn't even really notice them. "He's so easy to work with, Denis, it's never really a stress."Sounds like Pattinson will have the cool head needed to juggle his forthcoming roles - including James Bond. You could even say he may end up being shaken, but not stirred.

schema.headline: Robert Pattinson: How the Twilight star became 007

title: The young people caught up in Britain's Neets crisis
description: ByHayley ClarkeEducation reporterUpdated 2 hours agoThe number of young people who are not in work, at school or in college is both an economic and mo
body: ByHayley ClarkeEducation reporterUpdated 2 hours agoThe number of young people who are not in work, at school or in college is both an economic and moral crisis, a landmark report into the problem will say later. The 241-page report, by ex-Labour minister Alan Milburn, will set out a raft of recommendations for the government to consider. Ahead of its publication, four young people who are not in education, employment or training - those dubbed as "Neets" - tell us why they can't get a job and how the government could help them get one.Michael: 'Everything is experience, experience, experience'Image caption, We meet Michael after his early work experience shift at a supermarketMichael, 19, who lives with his dad in the Wirral, says he dropped out of college and spent a year at home after his social anxiety "got really bad". It is "very easy" to fall out of the system, he says, if there is little support available.Michael's story is not unique. There has been a large rise in anxiety and mental health problems in young people. About one in five Neets have a mental health condition, according to 2025 data, external from the Department for Education (DfE) - more than double the rate in 2012.Having signed up for Universal Credit, Michael was put in touch with the Merseyside Youth Association to help him find a job. He says mentors there have helped him improve his mental health, which led to him dropping out of college during his A-levels. He says that left him trapped inside his bedroom.He says jobs in his area are scarce and those that do come up tend to go to older people with more experience. Michael says he is trapped in the cycle of not having the experience needed to build more."Everything is experience, experience, experience - that's the one thing that I always used to hear when going for jobs on my own without the help," he says.We followed Michael for a day, meeting him after his 05:00 start for a work experience shift at a local supermarket that the Merseyside Youth Association helped him get.Image caption, Michael says getting his dog Dave motivated him to get out of the house and speak to people moreLots of Neets receive Universal Credit. For under-25s, the standard rate is £338.58 a month, external, which Michael gets. For some people who cannot work because of a health condition, disability or long-term illness, an additional £217.26 to £429.80 per month may be available.Ahead of the publication of his full review, it was reported that Milburn would recommend young people should no longer be able to claim those additional health-related benefits, as part of a major overhaul of the welfare system.Michael acknowledges some young people may be "taking advantage" of the benefits system, but says most "just want the money to get by so they can get a job".More recently, he has been doing shifts at the Merseyside Youth Centre's on-site cafe to gain more much-needed experience. His hope is to be in a steady job earning money this time next year, with space to have his own art studio one day."From three months ago I'm a different person," he says. "I can do stuff, keep going."Maariyah: 'I send 20 job applications a week'Image caption, University graduate Maariyah says she is getting turned away from voluntary opportunitiesMaariyah, a 22-year-old history and politics graduate, finished her university course last summer. Her dream is to work in museums.However, she is currently unemployed and looking for any paid job after working a temporary six-month contract for a housing association earlier this year.She says she spends hours each day in her local library - where she feels more able to focus than she can at home - submitting at least 20 tailored job applications a week.Those who have not achieved GCSE-level qualifications are more likely to remain Neet for longer periods - however, an estimated one in 10 Neets are university graduates. Maariyah says she is applying for roles in retail and restaurants, alongside unpaid work experience opportunities in the heritage sector. But she says she has also been rejected for voluntary roles because they had too many applicants, or because she does not have enough experience. "I'm actively going out of my way to do unpaid work, only to get rejected from these positions," she says.Not hearing back from employers "happens so often now that's it's like second nature", she says, adding that she finds it frustrating that many of her applications are likely to be screened by AI before a real person sees them. Image caption, Maariyah says she tailors her CV and cover letter for over 20 job applications a weekOn the day we meet, Maariyah heads to the job centre for her Universal Credit appointment after a library job application session. She says she has noticed an improvement in the support she gets there since she first received the benefit in 2025. This time, she will be getting some mandatory hospitality training, which she says she is "really glad" to have.She feels there is a growing sense of disillusionment among others her age. Being on benefits has become normalised because it is so hard to find a job, she adds. It makes her feel that going to a good university, getting certain grades and doing extracurricular activities "doesn't make a difference in the end"."I would like employers to give young people a chance to gain experience and take a chance on hard-working people who at the end of the day want a job so that they can contribute to our economy and contribute to their own lives."Matthieu: 'You might be surprised what people can do'Image caption, Matthieu has had many voluntary opportunities, but wants to find paid workMatthieu, 19, from Edgware in north-west London, is autistic and currently volunteers at a gardening club and a computer repair shop.We meet him in Finsbury Park, where he is helping to mulch some newly planted trees. Working in nature is calming, he says.He is looking for work with the support of the charity Ambitious About Autism and his mentor, Annie. He previously did a year-long supported internship with the Whittington hospital.Matthieu says speaking to people face-to-face there helped his confidence and he enjoyed being part of the team. At his family home, Matthieu's mentor Annie tells us that not having maths and English GCSE qualifications is a barrier to finding employment.Matthieu says he's more of a manual worker and wants to work in a factory, warehouse or doing deliveries, so that he can contribute financially for his family.Image caption, Matthieu enjoys volunteering outside in natureThose with learning difficulties, including autism, make up an estimated 12% of Neets, DfE data, external shows. Milburn's interim report, external, which was published in the summer, said 45% of Neets reported having a disability. He said the situation for young disabled people was "devastating".To make work accessible to him, Matthieu says he would need an employer to take their time with him. He says: "I don't learn that quickly." But he thinks it would be worth it."Honestly, you might be surprised what the people can do when you take the time with them and give them that chance," Matthieu says.Many employers say they can not afford to do so following rises to National Insurance contributions and the minimum wage, which is increasing further as part of announcements made in October's Budget.Some businesses have told the BBC they are struggling to provide new jobs for young people due to these changes, as well as other factors like rising energy bills.Although finding work is hard, Matthieu says he remains hopeful because of the support from his internship and job coach.Alex: 'Places don't want to hire us'Image caption, Alex says there aren't many job opportunities in her areaAlex, 20, from St Helens, has been looking for work for a year. She struggles with anxiety and is looking for roles as a cleaner or in retail. She also shares caring responsibilities for her mum with her other family members.We meet her at Spear, an employment and mindset coaching programme. Alex says her dream is to work with animals. She says she had been studying Level 3 animal management at college before dropping out last year because of her mental health."I was so burnt out," she says. "I was struggling to get out of bed, I couldn't do anything. I was dragging myself to college. I was like, 'No, I need to have a break for a bit and try and figure out what to do after that'."Building up her resilience is something she now works on with a mentor, as well as job applications.Alex says she is applying for "anything and everything" and wants to get off benefits. She is also currently receiving Universal Credit, which she says is "all the money that I've got until I get a job and I'm earning more".Image caption, Alex and her mentor, Grace, work on her CV during one-to-one sessionsWhen asked what she thinks about potential benefits cuts for young people out of work, Alex says not being able to access benefits would "make life so much worse".And she says trying to find work in a place like St Helens is harder, because many businesses in the town centre have either "gone or moved or shut down"."Lots of people think, 'well, young people just don't want to work,'" she says. "But we do. We so desperately want to work. Places don't want to hire us."Milburn has already said the system isn't working for everyone, and that serious action is needed to avoid young Neets becoming a "lost generation".Additional reporting by Branwen Jeffreys and Kate McGough

schema.headline: The young people caught up in Britain's Neets crisis

title: 'Complete reset' needed to get young people into work, says Milburn review
description: Sweeping reforms are needed to help 440,000 more young people into work, according to former minister Alan Milburn.Almost one million young people age
body: Sweeping reforms are needed to help 440,000 more young people into work, according to former minister Alan Milburn.Almost one million young people aged 16 to 24 in the UK are not in education, employment or training - or "Neet" - a current rate of 13%, which Milburn wants to fall to around 5% within a decade.His government-commissioned review, due to be published in full on Tuesday, calls for ministers to intervene from early childhood through to adulthood, funded in part by radical changes to benefits for young adults.But Helen Whately, Conservative shadow work and pensions secretary, said Milburn's proposals were in parts "too cautious" and too reliant on the "expensive hand of the state".Many of the review's proposed changes are specific to England, with some welfare and tax measures applying across all home nations.Milburn, a former Labour health secretary, says extensive change is needed to avoid a "lost generation", and address what he describes as a "moral" crisis.The review says that, in 2024/25, for every £1 spent helping young people into work or education, £25 was spent on youth benefits. By 2036, it says the aim should be for that ratio to be £2 on benefits for every £1 on work support. In order to make change of this scale over the next decade, the review will call for:A new target of 90% of children to be school-ready with basic life skills by five years old (this figure is now 68% in England, with a current government target of reaching 75% by 2028) More emphasis on work skills in the school curriculumInstant access to mental health support without diagnosisA doubling of the number of young apprenticesIncentives for employers, such as lowering the National Insurance rate for young workersAt the heart of the changes recommended by Milburn would be a legal entitlement to support, provided through a new "Youth Opportunity Service" in England.The service would put a young person in touch with a named adviser to help to secure them an apprenticeship, college place, supported employment or a job within four months.To pay for these reforms, young adults would no longer be eligible for the health top-up of Universal Credit, which provides extra money for people whose health conditions limit their capacity to work, or Personal Independence Payment (Pip), which helps with the extra living costs of having a long-term health condition or disability.The review's key welfare measures, some of which have already been announced, suggest replacing these benefits for under-25s with a new Youth Allowance at the current base rate of Universal Credit for young people, and a new Additional Cost Allowance to replace Pip.The minority of young people who are unable to ever work would be supported through a new Severe and Complex Needs Insurance. Kat, 21, from Devon, currently gets Universal Credit with the health top-up, so is potentially at risk of receiving a much lower level of benefits under the proposed new system.She has fluctuating physical and mental health problems, including occasional seizures caused by functional neurological disorder, which recently left her needing crutches.Kat says she "really wants to work", but says she has to rely on welfare support as she has been unable to find a job where she can be employed in a "safe way" because of her health.Milburn, a Labour MP from 1992 to 2010, says many young people are desperate for opportunity, but that many get knocked back repeatedly.Josh, 19, has spent three years looking for work while on Universal Credit with the support of youth employment charity Spear.Although they help him with applications to prospective employers, Josh says "none of them are getting back, and if they do they say you've not got the spot".Grace Coates, who manages Spear St Helens, says she wants to see "more openness to employing people with limited experience".Milburn's review will suggest gradually lowering the rate of National Insurance which employers pay for young adult employees to make hiring and keeping them more attractive.The existing Youth Jobs Grant, where employers receive £3,000 for hiring a young person who has been looking for work for six months, would be retained under the recommendations.So would the existing Jobs Guarantee, in which the government underwrites the cost of a paid six-month job.The government has recently announced that young adults will be eligible for the guarantee after 12 months of being on Universal Credit and looking for work, rather than the current 18 months.The Institute for Fiscal Studies has said reforms will have a greater chance of success if support for young people is balanced with incentives for businesses to hire them.It said that while cutting benefit entitlements would reduce the cash young people receive immediately, it might take longer for an increase in employment to make up for that for some young adults.Responding to the Milburn review proposals, the Conservatives' Whately said: "Where Milburn gets it right, we'll back him," but added that the review "fails to bring down the welfare bill, proposes billions more in government spending and won't make the slightest difference for young people stuck on welfare now".Liberal Democrat deputy leader Daisy Cooper said cutting national insurance for young workers would "only partly undo the damage of Labour's job tax".She said her party's plans would "shut off the Neets pipeline at source, with 100 hours of real work experience before 18 and a careers coach for every young person".Reform UK's shadow education secretary Suella Braverman said the 10-year wait to see changes from Milburn's proposals "would be consigning another generation to the scrap heap"."Reform UK would act now to axe Labour's jobs tax, double the number of apprenticeships and end university scam courses that laden students with debt," she said.For the Greens, deputy leader Mothin Ali said Milburn's proposals announced so far were "extremely concerning", adding: "There is an alternative to threatening vulnerable people with benefits they need, an alternative to unsuitable short-term work."

schema.headline: 'Complete reset' needed to get young people into work, says Milburn review

title: Sebastien Pocognoli wants patience but Scotland 'don't have time' says Andy Robertson
description: "First half, I thought we were in the game, we lost a stupid goal, but I thought we had chances and could have been 2-1 at half time," a frustrated Ro
body: "First half, I thought we were in the game, we lost a stupid goal, but I thought we had chances and could have been 2-1 at half time," a frustrated Robertson said, on the night he surpassed Kenny Dalglish as his country's most capped men's player."By the time you get to 50 minutes and you're 3-0 down, that can't happen in international football."It is a really tough night for us. I don't think you've got time in international football, you have to do it."These supporters who travel everywhere, are they going to give us time? No. Are the people inside Hampden going to give us time? No. Are the people outside Hampden who are going to be critical and rightly so? No."We don't have time, the players do not have time, we have got to step up."We have a long break now to March, which is not a good thing, and it is going to be a tough one to swallow."In contrast to his deflated players, Pocognoli put on a brave face post-match and insists he sees positive signs after his first two camps."The score is heavy with the 4-0, but I don't think it's a reflection of the game," he said. "We played a good first half, we created chances, we were dominant in some moments, and we faced Switzerland with different shapes and adapted well from the first minute. We conceded from maybe one of the first chances they had."At the end, it's a bad feeling, the score, but I think that the players try to do their best and create moments that we want to see."Again Pocognoli called for patience and the time which Robertson says Scotland do not have."The more we have games together, the more we will try to fix these things," the  head coach said. "We have a lot of good response from this camp and it's good for the future as well."But whatever Pocognoli's selling, former Scotland winger Pat Nevin isn't buying."If I'm ever in trouble and I need a PR man, I'm getting him because he's absolutely good at it," he said on Sportsound."He's certainly a glass-half-full person. You can talk away any moment and say it's just a moment, but it's four moments, five moments, six moments. "A really horrible thing in that situation is that if I am running the SFA, I'd be asking the players what they think and just saying 'tell us the truth... are you backing us?'"If a couple of the main ones say 'we're not sure of the decision-making' then I think it's got to that stage."

schema.headline: Sebastien Pocognoli wants patience but Scotland 'don't have time' says Andy Robertson

title: Thomas Frank: How former Spurs boss could restore his reputation and save Crystal Palace
description: "When the time is right I will look forward to my return as a manager, ready to embrace the job with great energy and dedication," said Thomas Frank i
body: "When the time is right I will look forward to my return as a manager, ready to embrace the job with great energy and dedication," said Thomas Frank in June.That time is now after the Dane was confirmed as the new manager of Crystal Palace, who are two points and a goal difference deficit away from safety at the bottom of the Premier League.Former boss Pierre Sage was sacked last week after just 16 league and cup games.The role offers Frank an opportunity to rebuild his reputation after he was sacked by Tottenham in February after eight months.Frank described it as "an honour" to be "in charge of this fantastic football club" as Palace announced his arrival on a deal running to June 2029."Crystal Palace is an iconic club in England and in the Premier League," Frank told Palace's website."I will do everything I possibly can to help and support the players and everyone around the place, and I'm really looking forward to meeting them."Palace chairman Steve Parish said Frank was the "perfect fit for our club".But how big is the challenge at Selhurst Park that awaits the man who made his name at Brentford?"It's going to be a bit of a shock for Thomas Frank," former West Ham and England goalkeeper Rob Green tells BBC Sport."He had his success at Brentford - a very well-run club where players are brought in with a lot of thinking and planning to take over the players they sell for profit."That doesn't happen at Crystal Palace."They lose players and then have a mad scramble to get players in. They have a team that has been decimated by sales and not replaced by the same quality."Thomas Frank needs to find something within that team that builds and garners the belief that means that they can compete in the Premier League, because it feels a long way short of that right now."Will Frank prove the right fit for Palace and haul the Eagles out of the relegation zone?Since getting the sack at Tottenham after 26 league games last season, Frank has been out of management longer than he was in charge of Spurs.In the summer he released a statement in which he said "there have been conversations and opportunities" to return to management, but that he had "decided not to rush into the next role".Frank's name was heavily linked with Palace before they went for a head coach with no Premier League experience to replace Oliver Glasner - the man who delivered an FA Cup, a Conference League title and the Community Shield before moving to Nottingham Forest."Palace had one of the best managers they have had, if not forever, silverware coming across the doorstep. Look at what they achieved last season and instead of building on that, they dismantled a team," said former Tottenham and England goalkeeper Paul Robinson."They have regressed."Frank once described managing as being on a "hamster wheel" and a "crazy circus"., externalPalace confirmed his coaching staff will include current assistant manager Paddy McCarthy and goalkeeping coach Andy Quy, who previously worked with him at Brentford.Justin Cochrane, who is part of Thomas Tuchel's England staff, is set to join.Palace are also in the process of approaching Chelsea set-piece coach Bernardo Cueva, who would join as assistant first-team coach.It is understood Frank would like to take Andreas Georgson from Tottenham, though the north London club are determined to keep the Swede.Denmark fitness coach Chris Haslam, who worked with Frank at Tottenham, is another potential member of Palace's new coaching set-up.A trip to Coventry City awaits Palace on Saturday.So why does Frank feel now is the right moment to return to management at a club propping up the table?Frank, who was part of BBC Sport's World Cup punditry team during the summer, will be coming into the job refreshed and with renewed energy and enthusiasm following several months out of the game.Between his appointment as Brentford boss in October 2018 and the sack at Tottenham earlier this year, he managed without a break for seven years and four months.Spending the past few months away from Premier League pressure has allowed Frank, in his own words, to "study, observe and learn from other leaders both within sport and beyond".Will his positivity and passion rub off on a Palace team who have lost seven times in 10 top-flight matches?Frank, who places a major emphasis on set-piece organisation, will have to hit the ground running at Palace, who have lost their past four league games.They have conceded more goals than anyone else in the Premier League (24) and have scored only 10 themselves."If you want someone to go in and restore some stability and defensive solidity while improving the set-piece element of the team, then Thomas Frank is the perfect man for the job," Times football writer Tom Allnutt told BBC Radio 5 Live's Football Daily podcast.With the Premier League season just 10 games old, Frank certainly has time to turn it around and will have targets in mind when the transfer window opens in January.Palace sold France centre-back Maxence Lacroix to Chelsea for £52m and Colombia right-back Daniel Munoz to Nottingham Forest for £22m during the summer transfer window.Allnutt added: "We know they have sold so many good players and so far I don't think they have really replaced them adequately."Another challenge for Frank is getting midfielder Adam Wharton, who has not played for England since March, back to something like his best form.These are all challenges the new manager will relish.After his bruising experience at Tottenham - having established Brentford in the Premier League - Frank has decided to climb back on the hamster wheel with Palace."Crystal Palace and Thomas Frank feels like a very good fit," added Robinson.

schema.headline: Thomas Frank: How former Spurs boss could restore his reputation and save Crystal Palace

title: Imran Khan seeks urgent medical care fearing he 'may not return alive'
description: Pakistan's jailed former PM Imran Khan has appealed for urgent medical treatment, saying that his and his wife's health has been deteriorating."At 74,
body: Pakistan's jailed former PM Imran Khan has appealed for urgent medical treatment, saying that his and his wife's health has been deteriorating."At 74, this unrelenting state is taking me to a place from which I may not return alive," the cricket star-turned-politician wrote in a letter published by his lawyer Salman Safdar.Authorities in Islamabad maintain that Khan gets seen weekly by doctors, who have assessed that he is of "satisfactory" health.Khan, who faces more than 100 charges, has been in prison since August 2023. His wife Bushra Bibi was jailed along with him last year. Khan argues the cases against them, ranging from corruption to selling state gifts, are politically motivated.Concerns over Khan's health have grown louder in the past year, with his family claiming he has lost most of his vision in his right eye after prison authorities failed to take action.In his letter, Khan wrote that doctors have told him he is "highly vulnerable to a brain haemorrhage and cardiac arrest", and that his heart has already "suffered damage".He also expressed concern for Bushra Bibi, whom he says suffered a detached retina in April and underwent surgery in secrecy. Khan said he fears she may lose her sight without further surgery."I have fought impossible legal battles in countless cases, and I have not stopped. But the system has stopped giving me justice," he wrote.He said that he is being held in solitary confinement for up to 22 hours a day, where he is allowed neither visits by his family nor access to books and television, and that this has "taken a heavy toll" on his mental health.He also claimed he had only seen his lawyers four times over the past year."I will only remain able to prove my innocence if I stay alive," he wrote.Pakistan's parliamentary affairs minister Tariq Fazal Chaudhry disputed these claims, saying Khan is "provided with all facilities in prison, including food of his own choosing"."[He] is currently the most well-accommodated prisoner in Pakistan," the minister told reporters.Authorities also say Khan was taken to a government-run hospital for an eye injection a week ago, where doctors deemed him "clinically stable".Khan, who previously captained the Pakistan national cricket team, served as Pakistan's prime minister from 2018 to 2022.His arrest in May 2023 sparked large-scale, violent protests by supporters, who ransacked the corps commander's residence in Lahore, smashing chandeliers and making away with furniture, paintings, and even peacocks, among other things.At least eight people died in the protests and the army were called in to quell the violence.Even behind bars, Khan remains a force in Pakistani politics. Thousands of his supporters took to the streets in early October in a dayslong march, demanding his release. Authorities later ordered a crackdown on protests and imposed a state of emergency in Khan's party stronghold, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa.Former international cricket captains have made several appeals in recent months to Pakistan's Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, insisting that Khan be given proper medical care.

schema.headline: Imran Khan seeks urgent medical care fearing he 'may not return alive'

title: Cass report author says she does not support draft conversion practices bill
description: The author of the independent review into gender identity services for young people says she doesn't support the current draft bill banning conversion
body: The author of the independent review into gender identity services for young people says she doesn't support the current draft bill banning conversion practices - having previously welcomed it.Baroness Cass said the current wording of the bill risked "serious unintended consequences" for parents of children suffering gender distress, or medical professionals working in that area.She was speaking at a parliamentary committee scrutinising the bill, which the government said would protect LGBT people in England and Wales.A government spokesperson said they welcomed her comments and would take all evidence put forward by the committee seriously as they "want to get this ban right".Conversion practices are generally described as interventions, treatments or activities designed to change or suppress someone's sexual orientation or gender identity.This can sometimes happen in religious or family settings and can be very distressing for the person at the centre of it.There have been long-running campaigns in the UK to outlaw such practices, and in its 2024 manifesto, the Labour party promised to introduce a bill banning them.When the government introduced its draft legislation, external in June this year, Baroness Cass was quoted in the publicity for it, external.In it, she said: "I am pleased to see that the government is bringing forward legislation which not only gives a clearer definition of what conversion practices are, compared to previous drafts, but also what they are not".She went on to say she looked forward to the bill receiving further scrutiny before it became law.But asked at the Draft Conversion Practices Bill committee if she supported the bill's current form, she said simply "no".Baroness Cass said the increased "polarisation" used in the debate around gender meant people may use the new law in a way that wasn't intended.The current wording of the bill requires the victim to suffer "serious harm to the individual's physical or mental health, or serious alarm or distress to the individual which has a substantial adverse effect on their usual day-to-day activities."But Baroness Cass said she worried this wording left open the possibility of "vexatious" complaints that could put therapists working with young gender-distressed people at risk of prosecution."If a young person, for example, has been sexually abused, any discussion about it is going to be incredibly triggering. "But if you can't therapeutically work through it without any reference to it, and that's the problem," she said.She said that professionals working at the new NHS Gender Dysphoria Clinics were concerned that even complaints processes that didn't result in a prosecution could be damaging.Baroness Cass also raised concerns about the possible impact the new law could have on families.She said that, for instance, if a parent stopped a child's money if they thought they might buy a "breast binder or hormones" that this may also fall within the scope of the bill and result in prosecution.Asked about her apparent support for the bill when it was first published, Baroness Cass said that she was in favour of the idea but hadn't had the time to read the details before the press release was to be published, but went ahead and gave the quote anyway.When she published her report on gender identity services for young people in 2024, she described conversion practices as "abhorrent". She says she still feels no LGBT people should be subjected to conversion practices.She told the committee she wants "a bill that protects the people it's supposed to protect, but doesn't accidentally entrap those who you don't want to [entrap]."The government said: "We want to get this ban right, which is why we have put this draft bill forward for pre-legislative scrutiny."We welcome both Baroness Cass's support for taking action to end abusive conversion practices, and her comments on the need for legislation to avoid adverse consequences."We will take all evidence put forward by the committee seriously as we move forward in ending almost a decade of delay for LGBT+ people who should never have to suffer abuse in an effort to change who they are."The committee hearings continue.

schema.headline: Cass report author says she does not support draft conversion practices bill
